transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Um, well, I came in because things have just been... really intense lately, and I'm not entirely sure how I got here. So, I just moved into a new apartment, right? And for the first few weeks, I was just kind of exhausted, barely unpacking, you know, just sort of existing among the boxes. But then, I don't know, it was like a switch flipped. Suddenly, I wasn't just unpacking; I was, like, hyper-focused. I started saying yes to all these mentoring sessions for junior designers, which I usually don't have the bandwidth for, but I just felt this incredible drive. And then I took on all these extra client prototypes at work. I'm a digital interface designer, so that's a lot of wireframing and user flow stuff, which is usually pretty draining, but I felt like I could just power through it all. And on top of that, I decided I needed to redesign my entire personal portfolio from scratch. It was like I had to fix my entire life, my career, my living space, everything, in just one massive sprint. I was staying up late, just totally consumed by all these projects and goals, and it just felt like I had to do it all right then and there. It's just been a lot, and I'm starting to feel a bit overwhelmed by everything I've committed to, to be honest.
Have you been feeling unusually happy or euphoric during this period of high energy and productivity?

Happy? Um... yes and no. It’s actually kind of hard to explain, because earlier this month, I definitely felt this... I don't know, this almost electric feeling? Like I was just vibrating with all this good energy and I was so incredibly upbeat. I felt like I was finally unlocking my true potential, you know? I’d be sitting at my desk, looking at my screen, and just feeling this immense joy and clarity, like everything was finally clicking into place. 

But the thing is, it wasn't just this pure, peaceful happiness. It had this really sharp edge to it. Because one minute I’d be feeling totally electric and on top of the world, and then the very next minute, if something didn't go exactly at the speed I wanted, I would just explode. Like, I completely snapped at this contractor who was supposed to be doing some minor touch-ups in the new apartment. He was barely late, maybe ten or fifteen minutes, which is honestly pretty normal for maintenance, right? But I just laid into him. I reacted like he was personally trying to block me, like he woke up that morning with the sole mission of derailing my entire life and ruining my momentum. 

And it wasn't just him, it was my sister too. She called me while I was in the middle of working on my portfolio, and she was just taking a little too long to tell a story—just a tiny delay in getting to the point—and I just snapped at her so harshly. It was like anyone who wasn't moving at my exact, lightning-fast pace was doing it on purpose to sabotage me. So... yes, I was really upbeat and euphoric, but also just incredibly reactive if anyone got in my way, if that makes sense?
Have you been sleeping less than usual during this period of high energy and productivity?

Oh, my sleep... yeah. Yeah, that's actually been really weird too. Because normally, I'm someone who needs a solid eight hours. If I get six, I'm a zombie the next day, right? But during this whole... whatever this phase was, sleep just felt like this completely unnecessary interruption. 

Like, for several nights in a row, I think it was maybe Tuesday through Friday of last week? Or maybe the week before... anyway, I was staying up until like 2:00 or 3:00 in the morning, just obsessively tweaking the CSS on my portfolio site. I'd be adjusting padding by like, one pixel, over and over, just totally wired. And then I'd finally force myself to lie down, but my brain would still be racing with ideas for the junior designers' mentorship program, or the client wireframes. 

And then, the crazy part is, I would wake up at like 6:30 or 7:00 AM. So I was getting maybe three or four hours of sleep, max. But I didn't feel tired! At all! I'd open my eyes and just feel this immediate surge, like, "Okay, let's go, I have so much time now!" I was completely convinced I was totally fine. I actually remember thinking, "Wow, I've finally trained my body to need less sleep, this is amazing, I can use all this extra time to get ahead on everything." 

I’d get out of bed, make coffee, and immediately jump back onto my laptop before the sun was even fully up. It felt like a superpower at the time, honestly. But looking back, I know that's not normal for me. I should have been crashing, but I just kept going and going on almost nothing. It was like my body forgot how to be tired.
Did you experience any periods of normal or low energy between these intense episodes of productivity and goal-setting?

Well, yes. That's the part that really scares me, honestly, because it's not just a little dip. It's like... it's like falling off a cliff. Before this whole super-productive, no-sleep phase kicked in, right after I got the keys to the new apartment, I was in this... this pit. And it's happening again now, which is why I'm here. 

It's not just feeling a little tired or unmotivated. It's this crushing, physical heaviness. I mean, I'll wake up after sleeping for ten, maybe twelve hours, and I still can't move. It literally feels like my body is made of wet cement. Just... dense and impossible to drag around. 

And it's the smallest things that become these monumental tasks. Like, I'll be lying in bed, and my phone will buzz with a Slack message from work. Nothing urgent, maybe just a junior designer asking a quick question about a hex code or something. And I'll look at the notification, and the thought of just moving my thumbs to type a response—just a few words—feels completely impossible. It's like my brain can't even send the signal to my hands. 

Or the apartment... I have all these cardboard boxes piled up by the door. All I have to do is break them down and carry them down the hall to the recycling chute. It's maybe a thirty-second walk. But I look at them, and I just start crying because I physically don't have the energy to do it. It's like my battery is at zero percent, and no matter how long I stay plugged in, no matter how long I stay in bed, it just won't charge. So I just lie there, feeling completely useless, watching the boxes pile up, watching the Slack messages pile up, and I just... I can't do anything. It's the exact opposite of that electric feeling, and it's just so, so heavy.
How long have you been feeling this crushing heaviness and lack of energy this time around?

Well, this time around... I mean, it's been a few weeks of this really intense, can't-get-out-of-bed feeling since that high energy phase crashed. But honestly? If I really think about it, and I've been thinking about it a lot while just lying there staring at the ceiling... these heavier stretches, this kind of profound exhaustion, it didn't just start with the new apartment. 

It actually goes back much further. I’d say I’ve been having these periods of just... total depletion for about eleven months now. Ever since my separation. That was when the bottom really fell out the first time. I remember it was late fall, and we had just finalized the paperwork, and I thought I was supposed to feel relieved, or at least ready to move on, but instead, I just collapsed inward. I spent almost all of November barely able to log into work. I’d just sit in my old living room, wrapped in this hideous gray blanket he left behind, and I couldn't even bring myself to make a cup of tea. 

And since then, it's been this cycle. I'll have these pockets where I feel okay, or even amazing like I did a couple of weeks ago, but then the heaviness always comes back. It's like the separation opened this door to this dark, heavy room, and I keep getting pulled back inside it. This latest move, getting the new apartment, it was supposed to be my fresh start, my clean break, you know? But instead, I think the stress of it just made everything sharper. The contrast between the high of finally having my own space and the low of realizing I'm still just as exhausted and overwhelmed... it’s almost unbearable. So, yeah, it's been about eleven months of these heavy periods coming and going, but right now, it just feels deeper than ever.
Have you ever had one of these high energy periods without feeling really low or exhausted beforehand?

I mean... I don't think so? It's hard to separate it all out sometimes, because everything just kind of bleeds together when you're looking back at it. But if I really try to trace it back, like, mentally map out the timeline... I'm pretty sure the really high highs always come after a really low low. 

Like, I can't think of a time where I was just cruising along, feeling totally normal, going to work, doing my wireframes, paying my bills, and then suddenly—bam—I'm staying up until 3:00 AM redesigning my entire life. It doesn't seem to work like that for me. It's more like... it's like a slingshot, you know? Like I get pulled back, back, back into this dark, heavy place where I can barely move, and the tension just builds up while I'm stuck in bed staring at the ceiling. And then, eventually, something snaps, and I get launched forward at a hundred miles an hour. 

Even before the separation, when things were just starting to get bad with my ex-husband, I remember there was this one time I spent like two straight weeks just crying on the couch, totally unable to function. And then, out of nowhere, I woke up one morning and decided I was going to master Python in a weekend. I bought all these books, signed up for three different online courses, and didn't sleep for two days. But that only happened after I'd been practically catatonic. So, yeah, I really don't think I've ever had the electric feeling without having the cement feeling first. They always seem to be tied together, like... like I have to pay for the energy upfront by being completely drained first, if that makes sense.
Do you always crash or feel extremely low after one of these high energy periods?

Well, yes. Yes, I do. It's almost like a guarantee at this point. The crash is always waiting there, right at the end of the high. It's like... you know when you're on a roller coaster, and you hit the peak, and for a split second you feel completely weightless, like you're on top of the world? But then gravity takes over, and the drop is just so sudden and so violent that it leaves your stomach in your throat. That's what it feels like. The energy just evaporates, completely vanishes overnight, and I'm left in this void.

And it's not just the physical exhaustion, though that's a huge part of it, like I mentioned before with the wet cement feeling. It's the mood, too. It's this overwhelming, crushing sadness that just settles over me like a thick fog. Lately, I'll wake up—if you can call it waking up when you've barely slept or slept too much—and before I even open my eyes, before I even register what day it is or what I have to do, I just feel this heavy, gray weight right here in the center of my chest. It's a very specific feeling. It's not anxiety, it's not stress about a deadline or a client rejecting a mockup. It's just... pure, unadulterated sadness. 

And it doesn't even need a reason, you know? That's the part that makes me feel like I'm losing my mind. The apartment can be completely quiet, the morning sun streaming through the windows, no urgent emails, no crises... literally nothing bad is happening in that exact moment. But I'll walk into the kitchen, and I'll see a single, unwashed coffee mug sitting in the sink—maybe the one I used the day before when I was still buzzing with energy—and I will just break down. I'll stand there in my pajamas and just sob over a ceramic mug. Because in that moment, that mug feels like a symbol of everything I can't manage, everything that's falling apart, everything that's just too hard. The contrast is so brutal. One day I'm redesigning my entire portfolio and feeling like a genius, and the next day, a dirty dish makes me feel like my life is completely over. So, yes, the crash always happens, and it's always this incredibly heavy, tearful, gray place that I just can't seem to avoid.
Do you always feel extremely low or crash after one of these high energy periods?

Yeah, exactly, like I was just saying a second ago... it really is a guarantee every single time. I know I kind of just went off on a tangent about it, but that crash is just so absolute, and I really can't emphasize enough how drastic the shift is. 

Lately, it’s been happening exactly like I described—I'll wake up in the morning, and before my brain even fully turns on, before I even remember what day of the week it is, I already have this... this incredibly heavy, gray feeling just sitting right here in the center of my chest. It’s like a physical lead weight that someone just dropped on me while I was sleeping. And the craziest part, the part that really makes me feel like I have absolutely no control over my own mind, is that my new apartment will be completely quiet. The sun will be shining in through the blinds, my phone isn't buzzing with urgent emails from clients about their wireframes, no one is demanding anything from me... literally nothing bad is happening in that moment. It should be perfectly peaceful. 

But I'll drag myself out from under the covers, walk into the kitchen, and I'll see that one stupid coffee mug sitting in the sink, and I just completely break down. I feel like I could just stand there and cry forever over this one piece of ceramic. It’s just this pure, crushing sadness that swallows me whole after I've been running so high, and it makes a single dirty dish feel like an insurmountable tragedy. So, yes, to answer your question again, I always, always crash into that heavy place, and it just totally paralyzes me.
How long do these high energy periods typically last before you crash?

I don't really know, to be honest. I mean, I wish I could give you a specific number of days or whatever, but it's really hard to pinpoint exactly when the high starts and when it ends, you know? Because when I'm in it, I'm not exactly keeping a log. I'm not sitting there with a stopwatch thinking, "Okay, the energy just kicked in at 2:15 PM on a Tuesday, let's see how long this lasts." I'm too busy actually doing things, or at least trying to do a million things at once. 

Like that time with the Python courses I mentioned earlier—I know I didn't sleep for two days, so that was at least 48 hours of just pure, uninterrupted buzzing. But did it last longer than that? Maybe? Maybe it started a day before and I just didn't realize it until I was already neck-deep in coding tutorials. Or maybe it dragged on for a few more days after the all-nighters, just at a slightly lower intensity, before the crash actually hit. 

It's all just kind of a blur when I try to look back at it. Sometimes it feels like it lasts for a week, where I'm just constantly on the go, redesigning client sites, rearranging my furniture at midnight, talking a mile a minute to anyone who will listen. But then other times, it feels like it burns out faster, like a sparkler that just flares up and then fizzles out in a day or two. I really haven't tracked it closely enough to give you an average or a typical duration. It just... it lasts until it doesn't, and then the bottom drops out.
Do you always experience a crash after one of these high energy periods?

I know, I know, we just talked about this, and I feel like a broken record, but yes, it always happens. Every single time. I mean, it's just so predictable at this point, but somehow it still catches me off guard. Like I was trying to explain before, it's this incredibly abrupt shift. 

Lately, it's just been so overwhelming. I'll wake up—and I use the term "wake up" loosely because my sleep schedule is completely wrecked by that point—and before my feet even hit the floor, before I even remember what day it is or what deadlines I have for my clients, I just feel this... this intense, heavy, gray feeling right in the middle of my chest. It's almost suffocating. And the thing is, there's absolutely no reason for it. I'll be in my apartment, and it's perfectly quiet, right? The sun is shining, my phone isn't ringing, nobody is demanding a new wireframe or a mockup from me... nothing bad is happening at all. It's totally peaceful. 

But then I'll walk into the kitchen, and I'll see something so incredibly minor, like a single, unwashed coffee mug sitting in the sink. Just one mug. And I will literally feel like I could stand there and cry my eyes out over it. It's like all the energy I had just a few days ago, when I was completely redesigning entire sites at 3 AM, just vanishes and gets replaced by this crushing weight where a dirty dish feels like the end of the world. So, yeah, the crash is definitely always there waiting for me.
Have you used any substances, such as alcohol or drugs, during or before these high energy periods?

No, no, I don't... I mean, I drink coffee, obviously, probably too much of it when I'm trying to push through a client deadline, but as far as actual drugs or alcohol? No. I really don't. 

I know sometimes people think that when you're acting like that—when you're up all night and talking a mile a minute and completely redoing a whole website's navigation structure at four in the morning—they think you must be on something, right? Like you must have taken Adderall or done cocaine or something to get that kind of energy. But I haven't. I really haven't touched anything like that. 

And with alcohol, honestly, I barely even drink socially anymore. When I'm in one of those really high-energy phases, I don't even want a drink because I feel like it would just slow me down, you know? Like my brain is moving so fast and I have all these incredible ideas for wireframes and color palettes, and alcohol just makes things fuzzy. I don't want fuzzy. I want that sharp, crystal-clear focus where I feel like I can conquer the world and learn an entire new coding language in a weekend. So, no, there's no substances involved. It's just... it's just my brain doing it all on its own, which honestly is almost scarier when you think about it, because I can't just stop taking a pill to make it go away. It just happens.
Do you feel like these high energy periods and crashes are connected, like two sides of the same coin, or do they feel like separate events to you?

I mean, that's a really good question, honestly. It's something I think about a lot when I'm just lying there in the dark during a crash, because... well, it's hard not to try and analyze it, right? Because they feel so completely different. Like, when I'm up, when I'm in that zone where I'm blasting through wireframes and I feel like my brain is just firing on all cylinders, I feel invincible. I feel like that's the *real* me, you know? Like I've finally unlocked my actual potential. And then the crash hits, and I feel like this useless, hollow shell of a person who can't even handle looking at a dirty coffee mug. 

So on the surface, they feel like total opposites. They feel like two completely different lives I'm living. But... but at the same time, I can't ignore the pattern. Like I said before, the crash *always* comes after the high. Always. I never just wake up one day feeling that heavy, gray suffocating feeling out of nowhere—it's always after I've spent a few days running on zero sleep and redesigning my whole portfolio or something. 

So, I don't know. It's like... it's like a pendulum, maybe? Or a rubber band? Like I stretch myself so far in one direction, pulling and pulling with all this intense energy and focus, and eventually it just snaps back, and it snaps back *hard* in the exact opposite direction. So I guess, yeah, they have to be connected. They have to be two sides of the same coin, even if they feel like totally separate events when I'm actually in the middle of them. Because if they weren't connected, why would one always follow the other so perfectly? It's just... it's exhausting trying to figure it out, to be honest. I just wish the coin would land on its edge for a while, you know? Just stay somewhere in the middle.
Do you feel like you're back to your normal self between these high energy periods and the crashes that follow them?

I mean... normal? What even is normal anymore? I guess... I guess there are periods where I'm not buzzing out of my skin, and I'm not staring at the wall wanting to cry over a mug, but... I don't know if I'd call it being my "normal self." 

It's more like... it's like this weird waiting room. Like I'm just sitting there, doing my work, talking to clients, maybe going to the grocery store, and on paper, everything looks fine. I'm sleeping a normal amount, I'm eating, I'm getting my wireframes done on time without having to stay up for 48 hours straight. But the whole time, in the back of my mind, I'm just... waiting. I'm waiting for the other shoe to drop. 

Because I know it's not going to last. I'll have a couple of weeks, maybe a month if I'm really lucky, where things just feel sort of flat. Not depressed flat, just... quiet. But it's an anxious quiet, you know? Like when the ocean gets really still right before a storm rolls in. I'll catch myself analyzing every little thing I do. If I wake up feeling a little more energetic than usual, I immediately start panicking, thinking, "Oh god, is it starting? Am I ramping up again?" Or if I feel a little tired one afternoon, I think, "Is this the crash? Is the heavy feeling coming back?" 

So even when I'm supposed to be in that middle ground, that "normal" space, I don't actually feel relaxed. I don't feel like *me*. I feel like I'm just bracing myself for the next swing, whether it's up or down. It's almost like I can't even trust my own moods anymore. If I get excited about a new project, I have to second-guess it. Is it genuine excitement, or is it the start of a high? It's just... it's exhausting. The whole thing is exhausting, even when nothing is technically happening. So, no, I don't really feel like I ever get back to a true normal. I'm just in between.
Do you feel like you're fully returning to a baseline state between these episodes of high energy and the subsequent crashes?

I mean, wait, didn't I just... I feel like I just tried to explain this, but maybe I didn't use the right words. Baseline. That's a clinical word, right? Baseline. Like the flat line on a heart monitor before things go crazy. 

But like I was just saying, I don't really know what my baseline is anymore. Because even when I'm in that middle space—when I'm not staying up for three days straight redesigning a client's entire e-commerce flow, and I'm not lying in bed feeling like a completely hollow, useless shell of a person—I'm still not really... resting? 

It's like I told you, it's this waiting room feeling. I'm sitting there, and technically, yes, my energy is "normal." I'm sleeping eight hours. I'm eating regular meals instead of just surviving on black coffee and adrenaline. I'm answering emails at a normal pace instead of sending ten paragraphs of frantic ideas to a client at 2:00 AM. So if you're looking at it from the outside, if you were just tracking my sleep and my output, you'd probably say, "Yes, she's at her baseline." 

But inside? Inside my head, it doesn't feel like a baseline. It feels like walking on eggshells around my own brain. Every single time I feel a little burst of motivation—like, say I find a really cool new font pairing or I figure out a slick way to animate a menu bar—instead of just enjoying that normal creative spark, I freeze. I literally stop and think, "Oh god, is this it? Is my brain speeding up? Am I going to be awake until Thursday?" And the same goes for the other side. If I have a slow afternoon where I just feel kind of sluggish and don't want to look at my screen, I panic. I think, "Here comes the crash, here comes the heavy gray fog." 

So, am I fully returning to a baseline? I don't know. Physically, maybe? Sometimes? But mentally, I never really get to just *be*. I'm always analyzing, always bracing myself, always waiting for the pendulum to swing again. It's like I'm a passenger in a car, and even when we're stopped at a red light, I'm gripping the door handle because I know the driver is going to slam on the gas or the brakes any second. You can't relax when you're just waiting for the next jolt. So, no, I don't think I ever fully return to whatever a true baseline is supposed to feel like. I'm just suspended there, waiting.
Do you feel like each high energy period is a separate episode, or do they sometimes blend together?

Blend together? I mean, I'm not really sure how to answer that, to be honest. I haven't exactly mapped them out on a calendar with a red marker or anything, so I don't really know if I have a clear answer for you on that. 

When I'm in that zone, time doesn't really exist the way it normally does anyway. Like, normally you have Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, morning, noon, and night. You have a schedule. But when my brain is firing like that, it's just... one long continuous stream of consciousness. I don't know if I'd call it separate periods or if they blend, because I don't even know what day it is half the time when it's happening. 

Like, for example, a few months ago I was working on this massive overhaul for a client's landing page. They wanted all these complex micro-interactions, custom hover states, animated SVGs, just a really heavy, interactive digital experience. And I sat down at my desk at maybe 8:00 PM on a Tuesday just to tweak a button gradient, and the next thing I knew, my alarm was going off for a Thursday morning meeting and I was still sitting in the exact same position, just completely wired. Was that one long period of energy? Or did it dip and come back up while I was staring at the screen? I couldn't tell you. 

So I really don't know if they blend together or if they're distinct events. Because when I look back at those times, it's just a total blur of glowing monitors and empty coffee cups and thousands of lines of CSS. I don't have a clear start and stop point in my memory. It's like trying to remember a dream, you know? You just remember the intensity of it, the speed of it. So asking if they're separate... I just don't know. 

I mean, how do you even define where one ends if you're barely sleeping? If I pass out for two hours on my couch, does that reset the clock? Is the next day a brand new period of high energy, or is it just a continuation of the last one? I've actually spent hours agonizing over that exact question, trying to trace my steps back through my version history in Figma or my commit logs on GitHub just to see when I was actually actively designing versus when I might have stopped for a minute. It's impossible to untangle. So yeah, I really couldn't tell you if they blend or not. It's all just... fast. Just one giant, fast blur until the crash hits.

Have you ever experienced one of these high energy periods where you felt so confident or invincible that you did something that had potentially serious consequences, like spending a lot of money or getting into a risky situation?

Invincible... yeah. I mean, money is usually the thing where that invincible feeling really catches up with me. It’s actually really embarrassing to talk about, because normally I’m a pretty rational person. I have spreadsheets for my freelance taxes, I budget, I’m careful. But when I get into one of those... those periods, it’s like the part of my brain that understands consequences just completely shuts off. 

There was this one time recently where I just felt like I was on the verge of becoming the most sought-after digital designer in the industry. I was looking around my home office and I just thought, "This space doesn't reflect my potential." It sounds so ridiculous saying it out loud now, but at the time, it was an absolute truth. So I decided I needed to completely redo my lighting. Because, you know, lighting is actually really important for screen glare and color accuracy when you're designing, but I didn't just buy a nice desk lamp. I bought these incredibly expensive, imported, architectural-grade light fixtures. I spent hours and hours obsessing over the exact color temperature and the drop length, and I just put them on my credit card without even checking the price tag. 

And it didn't stop there. Because I was already in this mindset of "investing in my empire," I went online and just started buying all these crazy expensive design software add-ons. Premium plugin bundles for Figma, lifetime licenses for complex 3D animation libraries that I didn't even know how to use yet. I just felt this overwhelming certainty that I was going to master all of it by the following week and double my hourly rate. It felt like I was making brilliant business moves. 

And then... I don't even know how I made the leap, but I decided I needed global inspiration. I convinced myself that sitting at my desk wasn't enough, so I booked a last-minute flight. Just completely out of nowhere. I decided I was going to fly overseas to just... soak up the typography on street signs or something. It was a trip I absolutely couldn't really afford, especially not booking it three days in advance, but I just clicked "purchase" like I was buying a cup of coffee. 

At the time, it didn't feel like I was spending money. It just felt like I was manifesting my future. But then, of course, the energy stops. The heavy feeling comes back. And I remember just sitting on my couch, ignoring emails, staring at these giant cardboard boxes full of light fixtures that I didn't even know how to wire into my ceiling, and I finally checked my bank app. And only later did I realize how badly it hit my savings. It was sickening. I had just blown through the safety net I keep for when freelance work dries up, all for software I hadn't installed and a flight I ended up having to cancel because I couldn't even summon the energy to pack a suitcase. It’s just... it’s so humiliating when the dust settles and you have to look at the receipts of what you did when you thought you were a genius.
Do you feel like you're ever truly done with one of these high energy periods, or does it always feel like it's connected to the next one?

I mean, "truly done"... that's a really hard concept for me to wrap my head around. Connected to the next one? I honestly don't know if I can even answer that. Because, like I was saying before about time being such a blur and not really knowing my baseline, my memory of how these things link up over months or years is just... it's so fragmented. 

It's kind of like having a bunch of different project files open on your desktop, right? Like, you finally close one, but is it really *done* if you know you're probably just going to pull assets from it for the next project? I try to think about the timeline of it all. Like, okay, I had that massive burst of energy with the lighting fixtures and the software and the flight. When the heavy feeling finally hit and I was just stuck on the couch, was that the absolute *end* of that specific energy? Or was it just... pausing? I really don't know. 

I've literally sat there in the dark, feeling like my body weighs a thousand pounds, and I'll wonder, "Is the engine completely shut off, or is it just idling somewhere deep down where I can't feel it?" Because sometimes, when the energy finally comes back weeks or months later, it feels like it's picking up right where it left off. Like, I'll suddenly care about those exact same 3D animation libraries again, and I'll pick right back up with the same frantic intensity. But then other times, it's a completely new obsession. I'll completely ignore the software and suddenly decide I need to learn how to code a custom backend database from scratch in 48 hours. 

So I really couldn't tell you if there's some invisible thread connecting them all under the surface, or if they're just isolated explosions. It’s something I actually tried to journal about once. Well, I tried to map it out, anyway. But my handwriting gets so messy when my brain is fast, and when I'm slow I don't even want to look at a pen. But I was trying to figure out... is my brain operating on a loop? Like in UX design, you have user flows, and sometimes they loop back to the start, and sometimes it's a dead end and you have to start a new session. I don't know what my brain's architecture is. I really don't. 

So if you're asking if they're connected to each other... I just have absolutely no idea. I don't know how to measure that, or how I would even begin to tell. It all just feels like my life, you know? Just this messy, unpredictable timeline where things just happen to me, and I don't know if chapter two is a sequel to chapter one or a completely different book. I just don't know.
Do you feel like each high energy period has a clear beginning and end, or do they sometimes blend together without a distinct separation?

I feel like... wait, isn't that kind of what we were just talking about a minute ago? With the blending and the timeline? Because like I was trying to say earlier, I really just don't have a clear answer for you on that. If you're looking for me to say, "Yes, it starts precisely on a Tuesday and ends exactly on a Friday," I just can't give you that.
